exercises.solution: `var` creates a single `i` for the whole scope. All three arrows close over it, and they are called after the loop has ended, when `i` is 3 (the value that made `i < 3` false). exercises.solution: `user.regular()` is an ordinary method called with a dot, so `this` is `user` and `typeof this` is `"object"`. The arrow has no `this` of its own; it uses the `this` of the place it was written, the top level of an ES module, where `this` is `undefined`. Output: `object undefined`. This is why arrows make poor object methods.

hints: `bind` returns a new function. Can a later `call` change its `this`?
exercises.solution: `bind` creates a function whose `this` is permanently `{ n: 1 }`. Neither a method call, nor `call`, nor `apply` can change it (only `new` behaves differently). So `f.call({ n: 2 })` still returns **1**.

exercises.prompt: `widget.refresh` is an ordinary method that uses `this`. Which of these call it later with `this` set to `widget`? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `setTimeout(widget.refresh, 1000)`
options.feedback: Not yet. This passes the bare function; the timer later calls it plainly, so `this` is lost.

options.label: `setTimeout(() => widget.refresh(), 1000)`
options.feedback: Yes. The arrow makes a proper method call, `widget.refresh()`, when the timer fires.

options.label: `setTimeout(widget.refresh.bind(widget), 1000)`
options.feedback: Yes. `bind` returns a function with `this` fixed to `widget`.

options.label: `setTimeout(widget.refresh(), 1000)`
options.feedback: Not yet. This calls `refresh` immediately and passes its *result* to `setTimeout`, which is almost never what you want.

hints: Ask of each option: when the timer fires, what expression actually calls `refresh`?
exercises.solution: Passing `widget.refresh` hands over the function without its object, so it is later called plainly and `this` is `undefined`. Wrapping in an arrow (b) or binding (c) both keep the link. Option (d) is a different bug: the parentheses call `refresh` straight away.

options.label: It looks for a `total` in an outer scope
options.feedback: Not yet. The inner `let total` already shadows any outer `total` for the whole block, even before its declaration line.

hints: The `let` declaration is hoisted to the top of the block, but not initialised.
exercises.solution: A `let` binding belongs to its whole block from the start, so the `total` in the template literal refers to the local one, not to any outer variable. But it is uninitialised until the `let` line runs, so reading it throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'total' before initialization`. This is the temporal dead zone, and it turns an ordering mistake into an immediate, clear error.
